title: Representation of data
overview: Summarise and display data using histograms and cumulative frequency diagrams, and calculate mean, variance and standard deviation. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Choose, draw and interpret statistical displays.
Use cumulative frequency to estimate medians, quartiles and percentiles.
Calculate mean, variance and standard deviation, including grouped/coded data.
Compare distributions using measures of location and spread.

definitions.definition: Frequency divided by class width; histogram area represents frequency.
Q₃−Q₁, the spread of the middle 50%.
The square root of variance, measuring typical spread about the mean.
A running total of observations up to a boundary.
An observation unusually far from the rest; a common rule is below Q₁−1.5IQR or above Q₃+1.5IQR.

sections.title: Choosing a display
content: Stem-and-leaf retains raw values, box plots compare location/spread, cumulative frequency supports percentiles, and histograms show continuous grouped distributions. Discuss what information each preserves or hides.
bullets: Use class boundaries for continuous data.
A box width in a histogram is not a frequency by itself.

sections.title: Histograms
content: For unequal class widths, vertical height is frequency density so bar area equals frequency. To recover frequency multiply density by class width. Label continuous boundaries and axes with units.
bullets: Do not leave gaps between continuous classes.
A changed vertical scale must still preserve area ratios.

sections.title: Cumulative frequency
content: Plot upper class boundaries against cumulative totals. Estimate Q₁, median and Q₃ at n/4, n/2 and 3n/4, reading horizontally to the curve then vertically to the value axis.
bullets: Graph estimates should match the graph's precision.

sections.title: Mean and variation
content: Use x̄=Σx/n and variance=Σx²/n−x̄² for a population-style data set in this syllabus. For grouped data use class midpoints, so answers are estimates. Coding transforms totals and can simplify arithmetic.
bullets: Compare both centre and spread in context.
A smaller spread means greater consistency, not necessarily better performance.

examTips: Write units on graph axes and quote comparisons in the language of the data.
Use unrounded variance before taking the square root.
Show the mathematical setup and exact working before the final rounded answer; unsupported calculator output may not earn method marks.
commonMistakes: Using frequency as histogram height for unequal widths.
Using class limits instead of continuous class boundaries.

quickRecall.question: What does histogram area represent?
quickRecall.answer: Frequency, so height must be frequency density when class widths differ.

quickRecall.question: Where is the median read on a cumulative-frequency graph?
Why are grouped-data statistics estimates?
quickRecall.answer: Every value in a class is represented by its class midpoint.

quickRecall.question: What two features should a comparison mention?
quickRecall.answer: A measure of location and a measure of spread, interpreted in context.
